title: Reading Comprehension Is Primarily a Function of Knowledge. It’s Not a Skill! https://davestuartjr.com/reading-comprehension-is-a-primarily-a-function-of-knowledge-its-not-a-skill/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that reading comprehension is mostly a function of domain knowledge, not a set of generic skills like finding the main idea or making inferences. He opens with a thought experiment in which literate people from thirty centuries would be baffled by such skill lists, and he contrasts them with the real strategies readers use when they want to understand, such as looking up words, rereading and annotating. Standardized tests with high stakes push teachers to drill discrete sub-chunks of understanding, making reading less natural and enjoyable. He lists the many kinds of knowledge a reader needs, from English orthography to historical sweep, and notes that individual knowledge makes any two readers' comprehension of the same text differ. His practical response is to build knowledge-rich curricula and to get staff to read about comprehension and decide what to start and stop doing.
points: Comprehension is simply understanding what you read, and it depends far more on background knowledge than on teachable generic skills.
High-stakes reading tests tempt teachers to teach to discrete skills like main idea and sequencing, which drains the joy from reading.
Authentic comprehension strategies, such as looking up words, rereading, asking questions and annotating, flow from motivation to understand.
The constructive response is building knowledge-rich curricula and getting every teacher to understand what comprehension actually is.
quotes: What would happen if we were to select a literate person from each of the past thirty centuries and ask that person to tell us which of the following reading comprehension skills is most important? What would they tell us?
Why do we do these things? Not because someone told us to, but because we desire to understand. We want to learn.

First, one of many troubles with standardized reading tests is that, since they ask students questions about inferences or main ideas or sequencing, AND since such high stakes are attached to them, we start teaching toward those discrete sub-chunks of understanding, and in so doing we turn understanding into something that’s infinitely less fun and delightful and dare I say natural. So the first trick is to NOT do that.

Second, the biggest predictor of strong understanding, whether from reading or listening, is NOT some historically new (and therefore unproven by 30+ centuries of human literacy) set of reading comprehension “skills” — it’s knowledge. This is true all the way through the reading process. Think of the things you have to know when you sit down to read my article right now.
We know that knowledge is inseparable from comprehension — so let’s start building knowledge-rich curricula. Is it hard to do? Oh yeah! I bang my head against it every day.

The first, mission-critical step is ensuring that every teacher understands what reading comprehension even is. If your staff doesn’t think this way, you’ve got to have them read an article on the topic and brainstorm a list of what to START doing and what to STOP doing.
